story: Kokopelli is a fertility deity, usually depicted as a humpbacked flute player, often with feathers or antenna-like protrusions on his head, venerated by some Native American cultures in the Southwestern United States. He presides over both childbirth and agriculture, and is also a trickster god who represents the spirit of music. Among the Hopi, Kokopelli carries unborn children on his back and distributes them to women, which is why young girls often fear him. He takes part in rituals relating to marriage, and is sometimes depicted with a consort, a woman called Kokopelmimi by the Hopi. He can be seen on the full and waning moon, much like the figures some see on the moon's surface. Kokopelli also presides over the reproduction of game animals, and is often shown with animal companions such as rams and deer. He is also associated with sun-bathing animals such as snakes, and water-loving creatures such as lizards and insects. In his role over agriculture, his flute-playing chases away winter and brings about spring. Some tribes, such as the Zuni, associate him with the rains. He frequently appears alongside Paiyatamu, another flutist, in depictions of maize-grinding ceremonies. Some tribes say he carries both seeds and babies on his back.
